stories.headline: Lula stages mass rally ahead of Brazil's presidential run-off
stories.deck: Polls show the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio, is favoured to win the October 25 runoff
stories.bodyText:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva led a massive rally on Sunday (October 11, 2026) to call for more days off for workers ahead of an election runoff against his right-wing opponent Flavio Bolsonaro.
A sea of people massed along Sao Paulo's Paulista Avenue, which was awash in red, the colour of Mr. Lula's Workers' Party.
The leftist leader, vying for a fourth term in office, is trying to regain ground on Mr. Bolsonaro who was the surprise winner of the first-round vote on October 4.
Polls show the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro is favoured to win the October 25 runoff.
While Mr. Bolsonaro has proposed a plan to cut public spending, inspired by Argentina's Javier Milei, Mr. Lula is looking to make improved working conditions a key plank of his campaign.
The Senate is due to vote on Wednesday (October 14) on legislation, approved by the lower house in May, to increase weekly paid days off from one to two, and reduce the maximum working week from 44 to 40 hours.
Mr. Bolsonaro "has to say whether he is in favour of workers resting more or continuing to work longer hours," Mr. Lula told reporters.
Mr. Bolsonaro has labelled the proposal as "opportunistic."

stories.headline: CJP leaders to approach police seeking date to hold peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar
stories.bodyText: New Delhi: CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka on Sunday said he and other leaders of the outfit would approach Delhi Police on Monday to seek a date for holding a peaceful protest at the Jantar Mantar, a day after three of its top leaders were detained at Delhi airport ahead of its planned demonstration in the capital. . In a post on X, Ranka said he, along with Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) co-convenor Saurav Das, legal head Ratna Singh and other leaders would visit the Parliament Street Police Station at 10 am on Monday to seek a date for the protest. . “Delhi Police can give us a date for Jantar Mantar in 24 hours, else the CJP will give another protest call,” Ranka said. . The CJP had planned to hold a protest at the Jantar Mantar on Saturday, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise. .Anti-CEC protests: Over 200 detained on Sunday as more mobilisation likely on Monday. However, Delhi Police detained CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, Ranka and Das after their flight from Mumbai landed at the Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport on Saturday. . The leaders alleged that they were forcibly removed from the aircraft and taken into custody without being shown written grounds for their detention. . Their detention came amid extensive security arrangements and restrictions across the national capital ahead of the proposed demonstration, with the CJP accusing the authorities of preventing the protesters from reaching the designated protest site. . The three leaders were released on Sunday after being produced before an executive magistrate. After their release, the trio alleged that their phones had been seized during detention, and that they were denied access to legal counsel, even as they vowed to continue their agitation. . Ranka had described the developments as reminiscent of the Emergency, saying trains were cancelled and protesters were harassed to prevent them from reaching Delhi. . The leaders also accused the government of turning their campaign against the Election Commission into a confrontation with the ruling establishment.

briefs.headline: El Nino sets temperature record in key Pacific zone: EU monitor
briefs.deck: Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later this year
briefs.bodyText:
An intensifying El Nino broke a temperature record in a key zone of the Pacific in September, the EU’s climate monitor said on Monday (October 12, 2026), in another sign the weather pattern is gaining exceptional strength.
Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode’s expected peak later this year.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an “all-time high” of 29.70C last month.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, “underscoring the exceptional intensity of the current El Nino”, the EU monitor said.
But in a statement to AFP, Copernicus said it “cannot yet say that the current El Nino is the strongest ever recorded”.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.
Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.
But the values observed in September “point to an already exceptionally strong El Nino, especially given that the event has not yet reached its peak”, Copernicus told AFP.
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.
On Friday, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”, with temperatures in the phenomenon’s monitoring area 4C above normal.
Record ocean temperatures
As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.
Overall, the world experienced its second hottest September on record, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27C, the EU service said.
September was 1.63C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900.
Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming “well below” 2C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C, in order to limit the effects of climate change.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.
“We are in a new run of months above 1.5C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027,” Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo said in a statement.
“Crossing the Paris Agreement’s long-term limit is only a matter of time. How far we overshoot, and for how long, is still up to us,” he said.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of “overshoot” above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.
Experts have warned that this El Nino would likely push global temperatures to a new record in 2027.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.

briefs.headline: ‘Put into buses, vans despite IDs’: Journalists detained again
briefs.deck: Journalists covering protests in New Delhi faced detainment by police during their reporting duties. Despite showing valid press credentials, several journalists were forcibly taken into police vans. Among those detained were individuals from established media organizations and independent outlets. The police reportedly acted aggressively towards journalists, leading to injuries and humiliations.…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: On a day SC said lawyers, journalists and other professionals should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties, several journalists covering the protests were detained for a second day running Sunday.
Among those detained were those working for established media organisations as well as independent online portals.
A photojournalist, who works for a news agency, told TOI: “I was covering the AISA protest at RK Ashram when police started dispersing everyone in the area. When only mediapersons remained, they started to drag us by our necks into police vans even after we displayed our IDs, our cameras and shouted that we were from the press.
The van had 7-8 journalists when they shut the doors and started moving. After a few kilometres, the van had to stop as police were removing barricades to make way. That was when I and two other journalists jumped out.”
Nitin Katiyar, a digital journalist with Nayab World, was detained from the Connaught Place roundabout while covering the students’ march. Showing cuts below his right eye, Katiyar said that police detained him despite his showing “valid media credentials”. 
He alleged he was pushed inside the bus, where police allegedly punched him in the eyes when he protested.
Among those detained were three Indian Express Hindi journalists. The organisation said in a post on X: “Three journalists from Indian Express Hindi — Shashwat, Siya, and Vijay — have been detained by Delhi Police while reporting. Even after informing the police that they were journalists who had come to do their job, they were forcibly put into a bus. The police bus was passing through Connaught Place in Delhi when Shashwat sent us a video he recorded on his mobile camera. Our colleague Siya’s phone has been seized by the police.”
The three were later let go at Chhatrasal Stadium, the media organisation said.
Pragya Mishra, an Uttar Pradesh-based journalist with Bharat Samachar, was also detained while she was covering the protests Saturday. On X, she posted a video of 5-6 policewomen grabbing her arms and legs while detaining her.
“Take people into custody. Make them sit in police stations. Stop those who are showing the truth. Don’t let the pictures of the rape of democracy go out. Delhi Police is working on this agenda. I have a mic, the mic ID is there. I have everything, but in an extremely humiliating manner, Delhi Police deliberately threw me inside the bus and detained me. This is the capital of the country...” she posted on X. A journalist working with The Hindu was also detained in the evening. Several YouTubers and content creators were detained throughout the day from different protest spots, including RK Ashram, Connaught Place and near Jantar Mantar.
There was no response from police over the issue till the time of going to press.

briefs.headline: Shikhar Mohan, another boy from Ranchi, who is making himself count
briefs.deck: Jharkhand opener Shikhar Mohan is making rapid strides in domestic cricket. After scoring 613 runs in his debut Ranji Trophy season, the left-handed opener has started the new campaign with a century against Kerala. With guidance from senior cricketers and a renewed focus on concentration and technique, Mohan is determined to take Jharkhand to greater heights.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Shikhar Mohan hails from Doranda, a familiar corner of Ranchi known for its educational institutions, PG accommodations and its much-loved litti chokha stall, whose popularity extends beyond the city limits.
“
Wo mandir ke paas wala shop... kaafi famous hai ab (That stall near the temple is pretty famous now),” said Shikhar, referring to Bhola Litti, a popular eating joint that he considers one of the best places for litti chokha.
The 21-year-old, who has lived all his life in Doranda, is arguably the hottest cricketing talent in India right now. Former India spinner and current Jharkhand State Cricket Association (JSCA) official Shahbaz Nadeem calls Shikhar Mohan a prodigious talent. "Lambi race ka ghoda hai, alag hi talent hai (He is a long-term prospect with exceptional talent)," Nadeem told TimesofIndia.com.
The second season is always more important because the opposition knows more about you. Teams analyse your strengths and weaknesses, so you have to keep improving.
Shikhar Mohan | Jharkhand opener
The opener has indeed walked the talk. After an excellent debut season in 2025-26, in which he amassed 613 runs at an average of 55.73, including two centuries, he has started the new season in rollicking fashion, smashing 143 in Jharkhand's opening match against Kerala at the Keenan Stadium in Jamshedpur. The southpaw also made some valuable contributions in the Duleep Trophy final for East Zone, scoring 85 and 52 in both innings, followed by a solid 60 on a green top in Srinagar in the Irani Trophy, playing for Rest of India against defending 
Ranji Trophy
 champions Jammu and Kashmir.
"I want to perform as well as I did last season. The second season is always more important because the opposition knows more about you. Teams analyse your strengths and weaknesses, so you have to keep improving," Shikhar Mohan told this website on the eve of their match.
Srinagar, Oct 01 (ANI): Rest of India's Shikhar Mohan plays a shot during the Irani Cup match against Jammu & Kashmir at Sher-i-Kashmir Stadium, in Srinagar on Thursday. (ANI Photo)
"More importantly, I want the team to do well. We reached the final last year, and I want us to go one step further. We have won the white-ball tournament (Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy). Now, our plan is to win a red-ball tournament as well. I want to have another good season," he said.
Shikhar has already made a great start to the Ranji Trophy season and credits it to the 25-day camp held in Chennai.
"We had a camp in Chennai for around 25 days before the Duleep Trophy. We trained during the afternoon in the Chennai heat. We also played in the KSCA tournament. Preparation has been on point," he said.
During the Duleep Trophy final in Chennai, Ishan bhai helped me understand which shots were appropriate for those conditions. For example, he told me there was no need to play the sweep shot in certain situations. He helped me understand what to play and what to avoid. That guidance made a big difference when I was building my innings.
Shikhar Mohan on Ishan Kishan
Shikhar admits that he was a bit nervous on the morning of the Duleep Trophy final. Despite training in Chennai for three weeks, it was his first time playing on a red-soil wicket. His state-mate and East Zone skipper 
Ishan Kishan
 helped him understand the conditions and guided him during the match. The duo put on 94 runs for the fourth wicket in the first innings and added 126 runs in the second.
"I spoke to Ishan bhaiya a lot during the last season as well. He would tell me which shots I should play and which ones I should avoid," he said.
"In the East, we do not get many red-soil wickets. We generally play on black-soil surfaces, so I did not have much experience batting on red soil. During the Duleep Trophy final in Chennai, Ishan bhai helped me understand which shots were appropriate for those conditions. For example, he told me there was no need to play the sweep shot in certain situations. He helped me understand what to play and what to avoid. That guidance made a big difference when I was building my innings," Shikhar added.
Chennai: East Zone's Captain Ishan Kishan, left, and his teammate Shikhar Mohan on day 4 of the Duleep Trophy 2026-27 final cricket match between South Zone and East Zone, in Chennai, Tamil Nadu. (PTI Photo/R Senthilkumar)(PTI09_09_2026_000191B)
Shikhar, who was selected for Jharkhand's Under-16 team when he was only 13, has been a prolific run-getter at every age-group level. He enjoyed back-to-back excellent seasons with the Under-23 side in the Col CK Nayudu Trophy. In the 2023-24 season, he scored 623 runs, including two hundreds and three fifties. He continued his run-scoring spree the following season, scoring 887 runs, which helped him earn a call-up to the senior side.
Despite his impressive run with the bat, big, headlines-grabbing scores were missing. Shikhar realised that he was experiencing lapses in concentration midway through his innings and received help from current Jharkhand coach Ratan Kumar and former Jharkhand veteran Ishank Jaggi.
Before facing a ball, I talk to myself. I remind myself to watch the ball and stay focused. That has helped me a lot. Ishank Jaggi bhai also helped me with this, especially when he was with the Under-19 team. I started concentrating more and focusing on one ball at a time. That approach has really helped me.
Shikhar Mohan
"There are two coaches who have helped me a lot. One is Ratan Kumar, who is currently our senior head coach. I also speak a lot with Ishank Jaggi bhaiya. He has helped me both mentally and with my batting. He was my Under-19 coach and helped me a lot during that phase. These two have played a big role in my development," he said.
"In my first year of Under-19 cricket, I scored around 550 runs, with most of my scores in the 70s and 80s. The following year, I wanted to focus more and convert those starts into bigger scores.
"Before facing a ball, I talk to myself. I remind myself to watch the ball and stay focused. That has helped me a lot. Jaggi bhai also helped me with this, especially when he was with the Under-19 team. I started concentrating more and focusing on one ball at a time. That approach has really helped me," Shikhar explained.
Chennai: East Zone's Shikhar Mohan plays a shot on day 4 of the Duleep Trophy 2026-27 final cricket match between South Zone and East Zone, in Chennai, Tamil Nadu. (PTI Photo/R Senthilkumar)(PTI09_09_2026_000189A)
During the Ranji Trophy camp in Chennai, Shikhar worked extensively on his batting, focusing particularly on playing close to his body, an aspect of his game he has worked relentlessly to improve.
"Before the season, I did a lot of batting drills. I focus on playing close to my body and working on my drives because those are the areas where I score most of my runs. I know my scoring areas, so I worked on them," the Jharkhand opener said.
"This season, I have concentrated on playing close to my body. I visualise myself playing within a box, keeping my shots close to my body. That has helped me a lot. As you saw in the Irani Trophy, the wicket was green. I kept reminding myself to play close to my body and avoid playing shots away from it. I think that is very important for an opener. You need to play straight because the SG ball deviates a lot, even after 10-12 overs. You have to be even more focused after that period. For the first 40 balls, my focus is on playing close to my body," he said.
Shikhar, who opens in all three formats, says his preparation for each format is different.
"The preparation for red-ball and white-ball cricket is very different. You have to go back to your basics and make adjustments according to the format. In white-ball cricket, you need to be more proactive and play certain shots regularly.
I remember a match against Uttar Pradesh at the Under-19 level. I was batting on 20 when a ball hit me on the chest. I went off the field and returned after we lost two wickets. We were chasing a target of 400 on the final day, and I scored an unbeaten 100. We fell 40 runs short when the day ended. That innings remains very special to me.
Shikhar Mohan
"Meanwhile, in red-ball cricket, you cannot play every shot in the same way. You have to work on the shots that are effective in white-ball cricket and practise them through specific drills. You need to prepare differently for each format and understand which shots are appropriate for the situation," he said.
Shikhar Mohan has played some excellent knocks in the Duleep Trophy final and the Irani Trophy, but the innings closest to his heart remains the one he scored against Uttar Pradesh in the Cooch Behar Trophy.
"I remember a match against Uttar Pradesh at the Under-19 level. I was batting on 20 when a ball hit me on the chest. I went off the field and returned after we lost two wickets. We were chasing a target of 400 on the final day, and I scored an unbeaten 100. We fell 40 runs short when the day ended. That innings remains very special to me," he said.
Young Jharkhand batter Shikhar Mohan (IANS Image) 
The youngster is already on the radar of several IPL franchises and has attended a trial with five-time champions 
Mumbai Indians
. "It went well," he said.
For now, Shikhar's focus remains on building on his impressive start and establishing himself as one of India's most consistent domestic batters. But with runs flowing and his ability to convert starts into big scores improving, the left-handed opener is beginning to make a compelling case for himself. If he maintains this form, a future push for India's Test opening slot may not be outside the realm of possibility.

North Korea fired projectile towards sea, South Korean military says
briefs.deck: While maintaining a hard line toward Seoul, North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems
briefs.bodyText:
South Korea's military on Monday (October 12, 2026) said North Korea fired at least one projectile toward its eastern waters, adding to a recent streak in weapons demonstrations.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff did not immediately say whether the weapon was ballistic or how far it flew. The office of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the country also detected the launch and described the weapon as a suspected ballistic missile.
The launch came days after South Korea on Friday (October 9) flight-tested its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defence systems, which President Lee Jae Myung described as an important step in strengthening the South's conventional defence capabilities.
While maintaining a hard line toward Seoul, North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems, including an Oct. 3 test of what the North described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
North Korea has also conducted other missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting U.S. and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy.
Tensions were further worsened after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border. The South's military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South's demands for an apology.

briefs.headline: Delhi-NCR wakes up to heavy rain, thunderstorms as IMD issues red alert
briefs.deck: Delhi experienced heavy rain and thunderstorms on Monday morning, leading to a noticeable change in weather. The India Meteorological Department predicted moderate to heavy rainfall for the next few hours. While cooler temperatures prevail, maximum temperatures are expected to range between 31 and 35 degrees Celsius. The IMD also forecasted partly cloudy skies and no rainfall over the next six…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Heavy rain and thunderstorms swept across Delhi on Monday morning, bringing cooler conditions to the national capital and causing waterlogging near Jhandewalan Temple in the Karol Bagh area.
The 
India Meteorological Department
 (IMD) warned of moderate to heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms over Delhi-NCR for the next two to three hours.
“Moderate to heavy rainfall accompanied with thunderstorm likely over Delhi-NCR during the next 2-3 hours,” the weather department said.
The morning showers brought a change in weather conditions, with overcast skies across the region. However, the IMD's forecast indicates that the wet spell is unlikely to continue through the week, with partly cloudy skies and no rainfall predicted over the next several days.
Maximum temperatures are expected to remain between 31 and 35 degrees Celsius, while minimum temperatures are likely to hover between 22 and 25 degrees Celsius.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a red alert for Delhi, warning of thunderstorms, lightning, gusty winds of around 60 kmph and heavy rainfall across all 11 districts of the national capital until 9am on Monday.
An orange alert has been issued for parts of Haryana and Uttar Pradesh.
According to the seven-day forecast issued on Sunday evening, the maximum temperature on October 13 is expected to range between 32 and 34 degrees Celsius, with the minimum between 23 and 25 degrees Celsius. On October 14, the maximum is likely to rise to 33-35 degrees Celsius, while the minimum is forecast at 23-25 degrees Celsius.
For October 15, the IMD has forecast a maximum of 31-33 degrees Celsius and a minimum of 23-25 degrees Celsius. On October 16 and 17, maximum temperatures are expected to remain between 32 and 34 degrees Celsius, with minimum temperatures ranging from 22 to 24 degrees Celsius. Partly cloudy skies and no rainfall are predicted for these days.
The weather department had also warned of possible traffic disruptions, water accumulation in low-lying areas and an increased risk of vehicle accidents in its advisory for October 11. Commuters were advised to check traffic conditions before setting out, follow traffic advisories and avoid stretches prone to waterlogging.
The IMD said maximum temperatures across Delhi had dropped by 1-2 degrees Celsius over the preceding 24 hours, while minimum temperatures showed no significant change. Minimum temperatures ranged between 21 and 24 degrees Celsius, and maximum temperatures remained between 30 and 32 degrees Celsius.
(With ANI inputs)

briefs.headline: Anti-CEC protests continue; journalists detained despite SC order, Rahul Gandhi announces march to Supreme Court as Delhi braces for fresh curbs
briefs.deck: Restrictions likely to return as Congress leader Rahul Gandhi appeals to all to join INDIA bloc march to the Supreme Court; epicentre of protest shifts from Jantar Mantar to Connaught Place
briefs.bodyText:
Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas and All India Students’ Association president Neha were among several protestors allegedly injured by security forces as they were being detained in the capital on Sunday (October 11, 2026), the second day of a protest called by youth organisations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Despite the Supreme Court’s directives on Saturday (October 10), around a dozen journalists were detained on Sunday (October 11) while covering the protest at different locations. There was no official announcement by Delhi Police on the total number of detentions on Sunday.
Leader of the Opposition (LoP) and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, announced a march to the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12), calling the “youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the Constitution of India,” to join the procession.
Security set to be tightened on October 12
The unprecedented security arrangements in the New Delhi area — imposed on October 10, and considerably relaxed after the top court’s hearing earlier in the day — are likely to be back on Monday (October 12) in the wake of Mr. Gandhi’s call. While mobile Internet was restored on Sunday (October 11), residents continued a cautious approach. Despite the festive season, footfall and business remained low in Connaught Place and the central Delhi area that was still interspersed with police barricades.
Activists of different organisations alleged that they were beaten by security forces, which the Delhi Police denied. The police claimed that the protestors were being adamant and not cooperating at the time of detention.
Meanwhile, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders who were released on Sunday (October 11) after being detained a day earlier, asserted that the protests would continue till the CEC resigns. He called Prime Minister Narendra Modi the biggest “coward” and urged people to protest peacefully wherever they were. CJP convenor Abhijeet Dipke left for Maharashtra to be with his family, following the demise of his grandmother.
New epicentre of protest
As security forces continued to block all entrances to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the capital, the agitation shifted to other parts of the city, with Connaught Place in the heart of the national capital becoming the new epicentre of the protest.
A series of protests broke out in the outer circle of Connaught Place, starting from a march carried out by various students groups, including All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) and the Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS), followed by a march led by AISA and then by the Revolutionary Workers’ Party of India (RWPI) and the Disha Students’ Organisation. All of them were detained by security personnel.
In the evening, women SFI activists doing a ‘Tiranga Yatra’ were detained from Connaught Place after 6 p.m. and taken away in a bus by security forces. The SFI termed the detention of women post 6 p.m. as illegal and alleged that the women activists were beaten by male officers.
By evening, security was stepped up in Connaught Place and security personnel detained many people, including some who were just talking to the media.
The CJP’s leaders, however, are seeking a return to Jantar Mantar. Mr. Ranka, Mr. Das, and Ms. Singh plan to visit the Parliament Street police station to seek a date for holding a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar. “Delhi Police can give us a date for Jantar Mantar in 24 hours, or we will give another protest call ourselves,” Mr. Ranka said.
Journalists detained again
At least seven journalists were detained on Sunday (October 11), from different parts of the city while covering the protest, despite many of them wearing their ID cards around their necks. Many of them were taking videos on their phones. The Delhi Police claimed that the reporters were working “too close” to the protestors while they were being detained and may have been detained because of “confusion”.
During the day, some student activists were detained in buses which had cage-like structures resembling police lockups, which is uncommon while detaining student protestors in Delhi.
On Saturday (October 10), 45 metro stations were shut down in the capital, while internet services were blocked around the Jantar Mantar area. Both the metro and internet services resumed on Sunday after a rap from the Supreme Court. However, residents continued to have a cautious approach, and footfall at businesses remained low in the central Delhi area which remained under heavy barricading.

stories.headline: 11-day Mysuru Dasara festivities begin with a traditional start
stories.bodyText:
The 11-day Mysuru Dasara festivities got off to a traditional start atop Chamundi Hills on Sunday, with Abhinava Gavisiddeshwara Swami of Gavimutt, Koppal, lighting the traditional lamp and showering flowers on the idol of Goddess Chamundeshwari placed in a flower-bedecked silver chariot on the temple premises.
The inauguration marked the beginning of a series of Dasara events, including the flower show, citywide illumination, Dasara sports meet, cultural programmes against the backdrop of the illuminated Mysuru palace, food festival, book fair and traditional wrestling bouts.
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and other dignitaries participated in the inaugural ceremony, setting the stage for 11 days of festivities celebrating Mysuru’s rich cultural heritage and royal traditions. For the first time, over 200 seers and religious heads attended the inaugural event.
In his inaugural address, the seer said Dasara, once a royal festival, had evolved into a celebration of the people and the land.
Saying that he did not consider himself good enough to inaugurate Dasara, the seer said he had come to the abode of Goddess Chamundeshwari with a prayer that the lamp lit by great personalities in the past should continue to burn. “I have come to pray for good rains and a good harvest, and for the happiness of the people,” he said.
Describing Dasara as a confluence of the past, the present, and the future, he said society should be built on values and ethics rather than caste. “Loving another human being as a human being is humanity,” he said, recalling Basavanna’s 12th-century message of Kayakave Kailasa (work is worship).
Recalling the Mysuru royal family’s contribution to the development of the region, the seer said the Dasara tradition could not be separated from the history of the Wadiyar dynasty.
‘We cannot download food’
Emphasising the importance of agriculture, the seer said technology might make it possible to download almost everything, but it could never download food.
“However advanced technology may become, we cannot download rice and sambar. We depend on the crops grown by farmers,” he said, calling for greater priority to agriculture and the conservation of natural resources.
He urged the government and the public to protect rivers such as the Cauvery, the Krishna, and the Tungabhadra. “We can import many things, but we cannot import water,” he said.
‘Contribute to schools’
Recalling educationist Harekal Hajabba’s contribution, who used his earnings from selling fruits to build a school, the seer urged people to support the development of schools in their respective villages.
“People from Karnataka who have settled overseas can contribute to building laboratories and libraries in schools, giving back to their homeland and supporting the State’s development,” he said.
“If all 6 crore people in the State pledge to work for development, it will mean 6 crore steps in the right direction,” he said.

stories.headline: 8,000 philately passports sold in a matter of few hours across Karnataka
stories.deck: According to the Karnataka Postal Circle officials, travel enthusiasts, philatelists and others lined up in queues of several hundred metres long as early as 2 a.m. on October 11, 2026
stories.bodyText:
A few hours after the Karnataka Postal Circle launched a new set of Philately Passports for sale on October 10 and 11, all the 8,000 passports in Bengaluru, Mangaluru, Mysuru and Belagavi were sold out fast. While Bengaluru sold 3,000 passports, 1,500 each were sold in three districts in two days.
According to the Karnataka Postal Circle officials, travel enthusiasts, philatelists and others lined up in queues of several hundred metres long as early as 2 a.m. on Sunday (October 11, 2026). Police personnel installed barricades around the General Post Office (GPO) in Bengaluru and guarded the place to prevent any untoward incident. People also brought speakers, played music and danced to vile away their time while waiting in the queue.
Recently, the Karnataka Postal Circle officials had announced the sale of 8,000 passports including 3,500 in Bengaluru and 1,500 each in three districts. In July, when the philately passports were up for sale in Bengaluru, all the 1,000 passports and 500 each were sold in three districts in a day.
A senior official from Bengaluru GPO, said, “We issued tokens starting from 7 a.m. and 8 a.m. Within 3 to 4 hours, all the passports were sold on Saturday (October 10, 2026) as well as Sunday (October 11, 2026). Some people who couldn’t get the passport were disappointed. However, we had already posted on social media pages requesting people not to start from their home to GPO as the passports were sold out.”
These passports were sold on first-come-first-serve basis and only one passport was sold to one person. Each passport has hundred unique pictorial cancellations and the cost is ₹600.
The official said that the fanbase for philately passport in Mysuru, Mangaluru and Belagavi is as big as in Bengaluru. Even people from surrounding districts queued up at these districts and bought the passports, braving large crowds. “All 4,500 passports were sold in these three districts in two days,” the official informed.
Yash, a travel enthusiast, said, “I waited for six hours in the queue to get this passport. Now, I have got another reason to travel across the State and explore places.” Pavan K, another traveller, said, “I slept on the footpath on Sunday (October 11, 2026) night and waited for eight hours in queue to get the passport. briefs.headline: Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation moves to open live bus data for smarter journey planning
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Bangalore Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) will soon share its live bus-tracking data, enabling better journey planning and integration with other modes of transport. This follows a similar initiative by 
Namma Metro
, which has partnered with the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC), a govt-backed digital public infrastructure platform.
An ONDC official said discussions with BMTC were at an advanced stage to share live bus-tracking data through the General Transit Feed Specification, a widely used public transport data format. BMRCL and auto-taxi aggregator Namma Yatri have already shared their data with ONDC.
“They (BMTC) have already shared with us their historical journey data; we’re analysing that database to find the margin of error and gaps. Even other utilities like Delhi Transport Corporation are on this platform,” the official added.
Commuters in Bengaluru can currently track Metro trains on the Purple, Green and Yellow lines with second-by-second updates through ONDC. A similar feature is not yet available for BMTC buses, for which commuters rely on estimated arrival times at bus stops and the Namma BMTC app, which is relatively less accurate.
Once integration is implemented, third-party applications will be able to offer more accurate bus arrival information and help commuters coordinate journeys across transport modes. Namma Yatri, for instance, already offers cab and auto bookings aligned with a commuter’s Metro arrival time.
BMTC ferries more than 40 lakh commuters daily. Sharing its live data could help improve connectivity between modes of transport and ease last-mile travel. Mobility activists have been demanding open access to BMTC’s data for over a decade.
“The new BMTC managing director, Raghunandan Murthy, has been very proactive in making this happen. Open data could open up many possibilities and transform commuting in the city, with the potential of AI,” the official said. The transport corporation had earlier raised concerns about the commercial use of its live-tracking data.
While no deadline has been fixed, officials are optimistic the integration will be completed by the end of the year.

briefs.bodyText:
What happens when passion meets purpose? For actor, artist, animal activist and filmmaker 
Samyukta Hornad

At an engaging interaction with students of BMS College of Commerce and Management, Basavanagudi, on October 9, Samyukta offered a glimpse into the many facets of her journey, showing how following her interests shaped the person she is today.
The session marked the launch of Bangalore Times on Campus, a new initiative by Bangalore Times that aims to take conversations with inspiring personalities beyond the page and into college campuses. More than 300 students and members of the faculty were part of the first interaction, which also coincided with the launch of Clock It, a brand-new tabloid targeted at Gen Z.
Making the presentation as personal as the journey itself, Samyukta used a series of cutely designed slides that she had illustrated herself to tell her story. From her work as an actor to founding Praana Animal Foundation, her journey reflected how a deep-rooted love for animals could evolve into a larger mission. 
Through Praana, she has been involved in animal rescue and care, including operating an animal ambulance service unique in the country.
Samyukta is now also exploring storytelling beyond acting, directing and producing films and documentaries centred on wildlife conservation and human-animal conflict. Giving the students a preview of this creative journey, she screened the first look of her film Crossing Paths, along with a still-in-production rap song that will feature in the film, offering a glimpse into her evolving approach to cinema and conservation.

stories.headline: When our meandering money leaves a mark
stories.deck: If every penny we spend leaves a digital footprint, what happens when strangers follow that indelible trail? For, a trail of transactions can reveal who a person actually is
stories.bodyText:
A cup of coffee, a grab of hot samosas, a premium movie ticket, the book you bought, a health insurance policy you opted for, a stock or mutual fund you invested in, a debt you cleared and what not? From the first Rupee spent to the last one of the month, our financial journey is increasingly out there in the open. Not just us; our money’s meandering voyage is also under the scanner.
Money has always left clues in every hand it touches. For instance, from the ledger books of ancient times, one could glean how affluent or frugal a family was, how much it spent, how much it saved and how much it borrowed. Yet, following such a manual trail, leaf by leaf through voluminous, timeworn tomes, was an arduous task, like tracing a tiny creature through a dense forest by the faint paw marks it left behind. In stark contrast to the dust-ridden ledgers, today, we live in the era of digital wallets. The money-paws of our transactions can be traced from mice to monkeys to monsters, all at the click of a button.
Where money once left a paper trail, it now casts a perpetual digital shadow. So, what happens when a stranger wanders into our digital woods?
To cut a long story short: If every Rupee leaves a trace, are we giving away a slice of our ‘financial privacy’? Every single Rupee we spend can reveal something about us: our tastes, interests, habits, preferences, priorities and even our way of life. A transaction may record an amount, but a trail of transactions can reveal who a person actually is.
Yet, safeguarding our so-called ‘financial privacy’ does not mean that we must return to a time when our money’s journey left fewer footprints. Once we progress, there is no looking back to the dusty past. No doubt, digital money is the way forward, and for predominantly good reasons: instant payments, round-the-clock access to financial services, automatic records of transactions, easier tracking of monthly expenditure, seamless payment of subscriptions, instant execution of investments, quicker loan processing, instant alerts for unusual or fraudulent transactions, handy proof of payments, reduction in the costs of printing or handling currency, and much more. Why should we lose all these advantages in the name of ‘privacy’?
Yet, on the flip side, the very convenience that digital money offers comes with a trade-off. The same digital trail that makes our financial lives faster also creates a vast pool of information about us. The question now is not whether we should leave a digital trail at all in the first place, but to know how we can use that information to study our own financial behaviour and be aware of what happens to the information left behind.
This drives us naturally to another question: who gets to see this information, and what protection does the law provide for it? The Constitution of India recognises privacy as a fundamental right; but does that extend to our financial lives as well? After all, the right to privacy is not an absolute right to live without leaving any trace. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 addresses this tension.
While the Constitution provides the foundation for our fundamental right to live with dignity and autonomy, the DPDP Act provides a modern legal framework to protect personal data in the digital world. Perhaps, the DPDP Act is a form of digital armour. It acts as a guardrail by regulating how our personal data is collected, processed and used. The law labels the banks, apps, and platforms that determine why and how our personal data is processed as Data Fiduciaries. Thus, the information in our meandering money trail is not a ball that can simply be passed from one player to another; legal safeguards come into play at every stage.
Let’s face it. We may not have much say in stopping the digital trails that feed external algorithms. Yet, we can turn the same trail into a money mirror: one that tracks our cash flow, spots leakages, curbs unnecessary expenditure and helps us make better investment choices. The trail that tells others about us can also teach us about ourselves. Perhaps, the real power lies not in erasing our money footprints, but in learning to notice them, interpret them and, ultimately, master our own money.
(Dr. Sincy Wilson is an assistant professor of Law and a legal researcher specialising in constitutional and administrative law. Dr. Vaishali R. Venkat is an NISM & CRISIL-certified Wealth Manager and certified in NISM’s Research Analyst module)

stories.headline: Festive phone market set to shrink in volume
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India's smartphone market is expected to witness a 12% decline in sales (by volumes) this festive season, even as the overall market value is projected to grow 5%, reflecting a shift towards pricier devices and longer replacement cycles, according to Counterpoint Research.
Rising memory costs have pushed up smartphone prices, prompting consumers to defer purchases or increasingly rely on financing and trade-in offers to upgrade their devices. The festive season, which typically accounts for a significant share of annual smartphone sales, is expected to be driven more by replacement demand than first-time buyers.
"The key challenge this festive season will be the size of the active consumer pool," said Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research. Higher smartphone prices, he said, are likely to keep many consumers on the sidelines, with discretionary upgrades being deferred and purchases increasingly driven by replacement needs.
The trend is also reflected in device trade-ins, which are emerging as an important driver of premium smartphone purchases.
"This festive season is shaping up as an upgrade season more than a first-purchase season. Fewer people are buying a phone for the first time, but the ones who are buying are moving up," said Sreevathsa Prabhakar, founder and CEO of Servify.
Servify, which handles over 3 lakh device trade-ins annually, said trade-in volumes in Oct and Nov are typically around 50% higher than in regular months.
Prabhakar said upgrades in the Rs 60,000-1 lakh smartphone segment are being driven largely by financing and trade-ins. Demand for above Rs 1 lakh, including foldable smartphones, is largely coming from existing premium users upgrading their devices every 12-24 months.
Trade-in demand is also expanding beyond metros into Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities, suggesting that premiumisation is spreading to smaller markets.The shift towards expensive smartphones is simultaneously boosting demand for device protection. Servify said premium smartphones have 30-40% higher protection attach rates than mid-range devices, with protection increasingly bundled with financing and upgrade plans.
With rising component costs limiting manufacturers' ability to offer deep discounts, attractive exchange values, easy financing and assured buyback programmes are expected to play a crucial role in driving festive sales.

stories.headline: FPIs pull out 44k cr in October, outflows in '26 cross 3L crore
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Foreign investors have withdrawn Rs 44,166 crore from Indian equities so far in Oct, bringing the total outflows this year to more than Rs 3 lakh crore as elevated crude oil prices, a firmer US dollar and higher US bond yields weigh on investor sentiment. stories.headline: ₹7.5 lakh crore private investment likely in nuke sector; 30 GW contribution by 2047: AEC chief Mohanty
stories.deck: The country currently has about 9 GW of installed nuclear power capacity and plans to expand it substantially by 2047, Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Ajit Kumar Mohanty said.
stories.bodyText:
India’s private sector is expected to invest around ₹7.5 lakh crore and contribute 30 GW to the country’s ambitious target of achieving 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, Atomic Energy Commission Chairman Ajit Kumar Mohanty said.
The country currently has about 9 GW of installed nuclear power capacity and plans to expand it substantially by 2047, he said.
"Public sector undertaking Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL) currently operates 24 reactors. We think private players should also enter the nuclear business and that is why new legislation was enacted," Mr. Mohanty, who is also the secretary of the Department of Atomic Energy, told PTI in an exclusive interview.
"Five years from now, I expect a couple of private sector players to run reactors. We think that about 30 GW should come from them by 2047. It costs around ₹25 crore to generate 1 MW,” he added.
Mr. Mohanty, who was in Ranchi to attend the 36th convocation of Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, said India was looking to accelerate nuclear power expansion beyond its traditional public-sector-led model, which would require substantial investment and technological development.
He said the enactment of the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act in December 2025 marked a major policy shift by opening the nuclear sector to broader participation by public and private entities while retaining sovereign control over sensitive activities.
Nuclear power projects typically take five to seven years to build, depending on the technology, regulatory approvals and construction requirements, he said.
Private companies are assessing reactor technologies, fuel supply arrangements, land requirements and potential partnerships, including joint ventures with NPCIL and foreign technology providers, Mr. Mohanty said.
NPCIL, a government enterprise under the Department of Atomic Energy, currently operates 24 nuclear reactors with a combined capacity of about 9 GW. Another 17 reactors, with a total capacity of around 13 GW, are at various stages of implementation.
Nuclear power is a capital-intensive industry, with a significant share of expenditure incurred during the initial stages of construction. The cost of electricity from new nuclear projects will be a key consideration for investors and power purchasers, he said.
“Alongside large nuclear power plants, India is exploring small modular reactors (SMRs) to cater to specialised electricity requirements, particularly in energy-intensive industries,” he said.
Industries, such as steel and cement, require substantial and reliable power supplies. SMRs could potentially meet captive power requirements at individual facilities or groups of industrial units, depending on reactor design, regulatory provisions and the commercial model adopted, he said.
The development of smaller reactors could broaden the range of nuclear power applications and provide industries with another option for securing dependable, low-carbon electricity, the AEC chief said.
Beyond capacity expansion, India is pursuing its three-stage nuclear power programme to make greater use of domestic nuclear resources, particularly thorium.
The first stage uses uranium-fuelled reactors. During operation, these reactors generate electricity and can also produce plutonium-239, which can be recovered through the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel, Mr. Mohanty said.
The recovered plutonium is intended for use in the second stage, based on fast breeder reactor technology. This stage is designed to support the production of additional fissile material and facilitate the eventual utilisation of thorium, he said.
“In the third stage, thorium is expected to be converted into a fissile material that can be used as nuclear fuel. Thorium cannot be used directly as a conventional reactor fuel without first being converted into a suitable fissile material. India’s three-stage programme is designed to address this technological challenge and eventually support a nuclear fuel cycle that makes greater use of the country’s domestic resources,” Mr. Mohanty said.
India has substantial thorium resources associated with monazite-bearing beach sands.
“Coastal states, including Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, have deposits of beach-sand minerals from which monazite can be extracted and thorium recovered through appropriate processing. India houses 25% of the global thorium reserve,” he emphasised.
The indigenously designed and built Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu successfully attained its first criticality in April 2026, marking the initiation of a sustained nuclear chain reaction.
With this achievement, India has officially entered the second part of its three-stage nuclear power programme. The milestone carries substantial global significance. Once fully operational, India will become only the second country in the world after Russia to operate a commercial fast breeder reactor.
India’s commercial nuclear power programme dates back to 1969, and over the years the country has developed domestic expertise in reactor engineering, construction, operation and maintenance.
At the same time, Russia, France and the United States have developed their own nuclear technologies, creating opportunities for international collaboration, subject to Indian regulatory requirements and project-specific arrangements, he added.
The Kudankulam nuclear power project, which uses Russian reactor technology, is an example of such cooperation.
“Further partnerships could help India access additional reactor designs and engineering capabilities as it expands its nuclear fleet,” Mohanty added.
India has signed Inter-Governmental Agreements (IGAs) on Civil Nuclear Cooperation for peaceful purposes with 18 countries, reflecting the growing global confidence in its nuclear programme.

briefs.headline: RBI measures: Rupee to gain sharply but forex liquidity likely to dry up
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Forex dealers expect a gap opening in the rupee-dollar exchange rate, with the domestic unit likely to record its sharpest gain in recent times. However, there is also a looming market freeze, with RBI's aggressive anti-speculation measures risking paralysis of legitimate market-making, choking interbank liquidity and inadvertently penalising genuine corporate hedgers.
Oil companies, normally the market's largest daily dollar buyers, will source dollars through RBI's special window, while stricter documentation rules could slow other commercial purchases. Meanwhile, RBI's dollar sales and expectations of rupee appreciation may prompt holders to sell dollars, adding to downward pressure on the dollar.
"While the weekend measures will support the rupee in the immediate term, liquidity in the forex market could dry up very quickly. Desks need substantial operational clarity from RBI before they have the confidence to quote two-way prices again," said Ashhish Vaidya, head of treasury at DBS Bank.
RBI's new 20% Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR) means selling forex derivatives to an importer client now forces the bank to lock up 20% interest-free cash with RBI. Because dealers do not yet know how or when this reserve will be debited, they cannot accurately price their trades.
One area where clarity is sought is cross-currency swaps, such as those used to hedge external commercial borrowings (ECBs), or coupon-only and principal-only swap structures.
In a foreign currency borrowing swap, repaying the loan principal is a capital-account transaction, exempt from the 20% reserve. However, paying periodic interest on the loan is a current-account transaction.
The question before banks is: "If an Indian company buys forward dollars to hedge its upcoming loan interest, does the lending bank have to park 20% cash with RBI on just the interest portion or on the entire swap contract?"
Locking up 20% in idle cash with the central bank carries an opportunity cost of roughly 6.5% to 7% in lost interest. Banks will pass this direct cost on to corporates through steep swap spreads, making standard hedging uneconomical for genuine borrowers.
Importers who prudently locked in forward contracts or currency futures to cover upcoming import bills are "long" on the dollar, meaning they gain if the dollar rises and incur paper losses if the rupee strengthens. If the rupee suddenly surges by more than Rs 1 against the US dollar, these long-dollar positions could incur substantial mark-to-market (MTM) losses, which the importers would have to cover.
"Slashing the threshold from $100 million to $5 million for derivative transactions without underlying merchant transactions creates an administrative headache. Instead, it would have been cleaner to simply draw a line between retail and wholesale market participants," said a dealer.

briefs.headline: Green cards not key to workforce strategy: TCS
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: TCS CEO K Krithivasan said green cards have never been a key part of the company's workforce strategy, as it has significantly reduced permanent residency applications for H-1B employees and stepped up local hiring in US. The company said the US suspension of green card processing would not fundamentally alter its talent management approach.
"In the last few years, what Sudeep (CHRO) and his team have been applying for is a single-digit kind of green card permanent residency," Krithivasan said.
TCS has been increasing local hiring in US, where locally hired employees now account for 50% of its workforce. The company plans to hire another 15,000 people in the country over the next five years. TCS had around 11,000 H-1B employees in its 30,000-strong US workforce.
TCS said its model involves employees travelling from India to work on client projects in the US for two to three years before returning. "There is a continuous movement of talent between onsite and offshore," Krithivasan said. TCS said fresher hiring would continue to be driven by demand rather than a fixed target of 40,000. The company onboarded 10,000 freshers in the Sept quarter, compared with 14,000 in the preceding quarter.
It has also increased its intake of AI-native talent from Indian universities by 50% as it builds capabilities for AI-led technology services. "We have increased intake by 50% because we find very good success in them being very natural. They're building great credibility with our customers and able to deliver outstanding results," TCS chief human resources officer Sudeep Kunnumal said.
TCS added 4,258 employees during the quarter, taking its headcount to 5.9 lakh.
The company's annualised AI revenue crossed $3.1 billion, accounting for more than 10% of overall revenue. Krithivasan said TCS was seeing a new category of deals, including those with Porsche and Best Buy, in which it helps clients rethink their operating models as AI changes business requirements. "We are not looking at it as acquisition of revenue or protecting revenue. These are two new classes of deals where we help the customers transform them fully," he said, adding that the objective was to help clients become AI-first enterprises.
TCS expects AI-led opportunities to offset productivity-driven deflation in traditional technology services, though a stronger net growth contribution could take time. Krithivasan estimated a six-quarter to three-year horizon for the balance to shift more decisively.
Technology spending could remain flat or see a slight increase as clients invest in AI, technology modernisation and business operations, he said.

briefs.headline: Rupee relief, higher hedging costs: What RBI’s new forex rules mean
briefs.deck: Reserve Bank of India has introduced new measures aimed at stabilizing the Indian rupee against the dollar. These changes include tighter restrictions on foreign exchange derivatives and new reserve requirements for banks. Analysts expect these measures to ease rupee depreciation and lower speculative dollar demand temporarily. However, external factors like high crude oil prices may continue…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The 
Reserve Bank of India
's (RBI) latest measures to curb volatility in the rupee could ease near-term depreciation pressure, reduce speculative dollar demand and help withdraw surplus liquidity from the banking system, according to research reports cited by news agency PTI.
The measures, announced through circulars on October 10, include tighter restrictions on certain foreign exchange derivative transactions and a new reserve requirement for banks handling rupee-linked currency contracts.
They are expected to make some hedging transactions more expensive, potentially reducing demand for dollars in the spot market and easing forward premiums.
Kotak Mahindra Bank said the immediate impact on the rupee could be favourable, although it cautioned that the global environment remained uncertain.
"The immediate reaction on INR is expected to be very favourable-likely move of USDINR towards sub-95 cannot be ruled out. Forward premia is likely to soften as OMCs and other importer hedging gets contained," the bank said in its report.
IDFC FIRST Bank also expects the measures to lower the USD/INR exchange rate and forward premiums in the near term, while noting that global conditions and balance-of-payments dynamics will shape the currency's medium-term trajectory.
RBI tightens rules on forex derivatives
Under the October 10 circulars, the RBI barred authorised dealers from allowing users to rebook cancelled rupee-linked foreign exchange derivative contracts. Rollovers at maturity remain permitted, subject to existing regulations.
The central bank also lowered the threshold for undertaking foreign exchange derivative transactions without establishing an underlying exposure to $5 million from $100 million. The revised limit applies across authorised dealers and recognised stock exchanges.
In another measure, the RBI introduced a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR). Authorised dealers must maintain the reserve with the central bank in cash, amounting to 20 per cent of the rupee equivalent of the notional value of each rupee-linked foreign exchange derivative contract exceeding $2 million, where the transaction hedges current account exposure involving the purchase of foreign currency against the rupee.
The RBI said the measures were intended to strengthen market discipline, ensure appropriate risk management and maintain an orderly and transparent foreign exchange market.
Higher hedging costs could curb dollar demand
The new reserve requirement could raise the cost of hedging currency exposure for importers, potentially discouraging some transactions and reducing demand for dollars.
Kotak Mahindra Bank estimates that hedging costs could rise by 1-1.6 per cent, while IDFC FIRST Bank expects an increase of around 1.5 per cent.
However, the relief to the rupee could be limited if external pressures persist. IDFC FIRST Bank identified elevated crude oil prices, foreign portfolio outflows and weak underlying capital flows as factors that could continue to weigh on the currency.
The measures could also influence the RBI's interest-rate decisions. IDFC FIRST Bank said that if the steps ease depreciation pressure by curbing speculative demand and changing hedging behaviour, the central bank could adopt a gradual approach to further rate increases.
The bank expects the terminal repo rate to be in the range of 6-6.25 per cent. The RBI raised the repo rate by 25 basis points at its October monetary policy meeting and shifted its stance to calibrated tightening.
Banks expect further withdrawal of liquidity
The RBI's foreign exchange measures could also contribute to a reduction in surplus liquidity in the banking system.
IDFC FIRST Bank estimates that core liquidity surplus could decline to around Rs 2 lakh crore by March 2027 from Rs 10.4 lakh crore on October 2, as currency leakage and balance-of-payments pressures add to the impact of the central bank's liquidity operations.
Kotak Mahindra Bank estimates that the measures could withdraw around Rs 1.5 lakh crore of durable liquidity if they remain in force for another month. The bank also expects further liquidity withdrawal through open market bond sales and foreign exchange intervention.
The RBI has announced an open market sale of government securities worth Rs 25,000 crore for October, following earlier liquidity-draining operations.
It has also increased the daily maintenance requirement for the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to 99 per cent from 90 per cent following a review of liquidity conditions.

briefs.headline: Homebuyer paid Rs 39.15 lakh but got no flat; RERA rejects builder's excuse orders interest payout
briefs.deck: The homebuyer alleged that the builder had invoked the PMRDA-PMC jurisdiction dispute only after the delay happened, using it as an excuse to explain why the flat had not been handed over to the buyer on time. The flat was priced at Rs 41.85 lakh, and the buyer had paid Rs 39.15 lakh. The remaining amount can be adjusted against the interest payable by the developer.
briefs.bodyText:
When buying your dream home, timely possession is an important point. Yet in some cases builders fail to deliver flats and houses within the stipulated time period.
In one such recent case, the Maharashtra Real Estate Regulatory Authority (MahaRERA) has ruled that a builder cannot escape responsibility for delaying possession of flats by blaming administrative changes involving government authorities when the delay stems from its own failure.
What the case is about
A man bought a flat from a builder but did not get possession of it in the promised time period in the sale agreement.
The builder, on its part, claimed that the delay was due to changes in government jurisdiction. The builder argued that, during 2022-2023, planning authority over Wagholi, where the project is located, shifted between the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) and the Pune Metropolitan Region Development Authority (PMRDA).
Also Read | 
Woman buys Rs 1.03 crore 3BHK in Bengaluru, but builder fails to provide specially-enabled parking; Karnataka RERA orders provision within 60 days and audited maintenance accounts
According to the builder, this change led to revised plans and fresh approvals, which held up the construction.
The homebuyer, however, challenged this explanation before the MahaRERA tribunal by filing a rejoinder. He submitted documents to argue that the builder already knew Wagholi fell under PMC's jurisdiction before the sale agreement was executed.
The homebuyer relied on a notification issued by the Urban Development Department (UDD) on June 30, 2021, which clearly placed Wagholi under PMC's jurisdiction.
The homebuyer also pointed out that the plans for Wing C of the project, in which he had purchased a flat, had been approved by the RERA authority in January 2022. The sale agreement was then signed in September 2022, with possession scheduled for December 2024.
The homebuyer alleged that the builder had invoked the PMRDA-PMC jurisdiction dispute only after the delay happened, using it as an excuse to explain why the flat had not been handed over to the buyer on time.
Defending its position before the MahaRERA tribunal, the builder said it had offered compensation of Rs 35,000 as a goodwill gesture, without accepting liability for any inconvenience caused to the homebuyer.
Also Read | 
Man invested Rs 10 lakh, which tax department treated as unexplained; he first cited cash loan, then bank withdrawals as source, ITAT Nagpur deletes addition and Rs 2.11 lakh penalty
Why did the homebuyer win the case?
In an order dated September 8, 2026, MahaRERA directed the developer to pay interest from January 1, 2025, until it hands over possession with the required Occupancy Certificate.
The Maharashtra Real Estate Regulatory Authority (MahaRERA) rejected the builder’s explanation that changes involving the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) and Pune Metropolitan Region Development Authority (PMRDA) had held up approvals for its Wagholi project.
The buyer relied on a June 30, 2021 notification from the state Urban Development Department that placed Wagholi under PMC’s jurisdiction.
The authority did not accept the builder’s explanation as adequate justification for missing the agreed deadline. Securing approvals and obtaining the certificates required for a lawful handover remained the developer’s responsibility. It also needed credible evidence linking the administrative difficulties it cited to the delay.
Also Read | 
Grandmother and her son gifted 2.5-acre land to his second wife, who sold it; his daughter from first marriage claimed it was ancestral, but Madras HC rejects her plea
The builder had offered Rs 35,000 as a goodwill gesture, without admitting liability. That offer did not settle the matter. Under Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, a homebuyer can seek relief when a promoter fails to meet its obligations relating to completion or possession. MahaRERA held the developer liable under this provision.
Aradhana Bhansali, Senior Partner at Rajani Associates, told ET that the buyer had succeeded because possession was not delivered within the timeline set out in the registered Agreement for Sale.
The flat was priced at Rs 41.85 lakh, and the buyer had paid Rs 39.15 lakh. The remaining amount can be adjusted against the interest payable by the developer. The interest rate specified in the order is SBI’s marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) plus 2%.
The interest liability continues until the developer hands over the flat with the required Occupancy Certificate.
